input.name: linearRecurrenceSum
input.signature: linearRecurrenceSum(a0, a1, p, q, n, m) -> string
input.task: Define a sequence by a(0) = a0, a(1) = a1 and a(k) = p*a(k-1) + q*a(k-2) for k >= 2. Return the sum a(0) + a(1) + ... + a(n), reduced modulo m, as a decimal string. a0, a1, p and q are integers (numbers) with absolute value at most 1000000000; they can be negative. n is a non-negative integer given as a decimal string, up to 10^18. m is an integer from 1 to 1000000000. The answer is always in the range 0 to m-1: a negative sum is brought into that range (the sum -1 with m = 7 gives "6"). When n is "0" the sum is a0 reduced modulo m. When m is 1 the answer is "0".

input.name: countDistinctNeighbours
input.task: Count the integers x with lo <= x <= hi that satisfy both rules. Rule 1: no two neighbouring decimal digits of x are equal (the number 0 has one digit, so it passes; 100 fails; 121 passes). Rule 2: the sum of the decimal digits of x is divisible by k (0 has digit sum 0, which every k divides). lo and hi are non-negative integers given as decimal strings without leading zeros, up to 10^18. If lo is greater than hi the answer is 0. k is an integer (a number) from 1 to 60. Return the count as a decimal string. Example: lo "0", hi "20", k 3 gives "7" (the numbers 0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 and 18).

edges.lo-above-hi: If lo is greater than hi

input.name: countNotDivisible
input.task: Count the integers x with lo <= x <= hi that are divisible by none of the numbers in primes. primes is an array of distinct prime numbers (each from 2 to 1000, at most 14 entries, in any order); it can be empty. lo and hi are integers given as decimal strings; they can be negative and their absolute value is at most 10^18. If lo is greater than hi the answer is 0. Zero is divisible by every prime, so 0 is never counted when primes is not empty; when primes is empty, every integer in the range counts, including 0. A negative number is divisible by p when its absolute value is. Return the count as a decimal string.

edges.zero-not-counted: Zero is divisible by every prime
edges.negative-divisible: A negative number is divisible by p
edges.lo-above-hi: If lo is greater than hi

input.name: countPathsAvoiding
input.task: Count the paths on the integer grid from (0, 0) to (w, h) in which every step moves one unit right (x + 1) or one unit up (y + 1), and no visited point (the start and the end included) is in blocked. w and h are integers from 0 to 1000000. blocked is an array of [x, y] integer pairs with at most 12 entries; it can contain the same point twice, and points outside the rectangle 0 <= x <= w, 0 <= y <= h (they can have negative coordinates) block nothing. If the start or the end is blocked the answer is 0. Return the number of paths modulo 1000000007 as a number.

edges.start-or-end: If the start or the end is blocked

input.name: kthPlainNumber
input.task: The positive integers that are neither a perfect square nor a perfect cube, taken in increasing order, form the sequence 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 17, 18, ... (1 and 64 are both a square and a cube; 4, 9 and 16 are squares; 8 and 27 are cubes; none of these appear). Return the k-th term of this sequence as a decimal string. k is given as a decimal string with 1 <= k <= 10^18.

edges.square-and-cube: both a square and a cube

input.name: squareDigit
input.task: Write the squares of the positive integers one after another with no separator: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, ... gives the infinite digit string that begins 149162536496481100121144. Return the n-th digit of this string (counting from 1) as a one-character string. n is a decimal string with 1 <= n <= 10^18.

edges.digit-count-change: one after another with no separator

input.name: shuffleN
input.task: items is an array of L values (1 <= L <= 300; the values can be of any JSON type, and some can be equal). a and b are arrays that are each a permutation of the numbers 0 .. L-1. One step with a permutation perm turns the current array cur into a new array next, where next[i] = cur[perm[i]] for every index i. The steps are numbered from 1: the odd steps (1, 3, 5, ...) use the permutation a and the even steps (2, 4, 6, ...) use the permutation b. n is a decimal string with 0 <= n <= 10^18. Return the array after n steps, starting from items. When n is "0" return a copy of items. Do not change the arguments.

edges.alternate: the odd steps (1, 3, 5, ...) use the permutation a

input.name: closestFraction
input.task: Find the fraction a/b closest to p/q among all fractions whose denominator b is an integer from 1 to maxDen (the numerator a can be any integer, also zero or negative). p, q and maxDen are decimal strings: p is an integer (it can be negative, absolute value at most 10^30), q is a positive integer at most 10^30, and maxDen is an integer from 1 to 10^30. Closeness is the exact absolute difference |a/b - p/q|. If two different fractions are equally close, choose the one with the smaller denominator; if the denominators are equal too, choose the smaller value. Return the answer in lowest terms as "a/b", always with the slash and the denominator, even when it is 1 ("3/1", "0/1", "-2/1"). When p/q itself can be written with a denominator of at most maxDen, return exactly p/q in lowest terms.

edges.tie-smaller-denominator: choose the one with the smaller denominator
edges.exact: When p/q itself can be written
edges.slash-always: always with the slash and the denominator

input.name: parseDialectCsv

edges.doubled-quote: two single quotes in a row
edges.after-close: anything else makes the text invalid

input.name: evalExpr
input.task: Evaluate an integer arithmetic expression and return the result as a decimal string, or the string "ERR" when the expression is invalid or cannot be evaluated. Tokens: non-negative decimal integers (leading zeros are allowed: "007" is 7), the operators + - * / % ^, parentheses, and spaces, tabs or line breaks between tokens (they are ignored). Any other character makes the result "ERR". Precedence from loosest to tightest: (1) binary + and -, left to right; (2) binary *, / and %, left to right; (3) unary minus, a minus sign in front of an operand, which can repeat ("--3" is 3); (4) ^, which is right-associative. So unary minus applies to the whole power on its right: "-2^2" is -4 and "2^3^2" is 512. The exponent of ^ can itself start with unary minus signs: "2^--1" is 2, and "2^-1" is an error because the exponent is negative. There is no unary plus ("+3" is "ERR"). / is integer division that truncates toward zero (7/-2 is -3, -7/2 is -3). % is the remainder of that division, so it has the sign of the left operand (-7%3 is -1, 7%-3 is 1). Division or remainder by zero gives "ERR". The exponent must be an integer from 0 to 1000, otherwise the result is "ERR"; 0^0 is 1. Integers have no size limit (2^100 is 1267650600228229401496703205376). An error anywhere in the expression makes the whole result "ERR", even in a part that a normal reading would not need. An empty expression, an unbalanced parenthesis, empty parentheses, a missing operand and two operands in a row ("1 2") are all "ERR". A result of zero is "0", never "-0".

edges.unary-minus-power: unary minus applies to the whole power
edges.error-anywhere: An error anywhere in the expression

input.name: satisfiesRange
input.task: Return true when version satisfies range, otherwise false. Return false when version or any part of range is malformed. A version is MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH with an optional prerelease after a hyphen and optional build metadata after a plus sign, for example 1.2.3, 1.2.3-beta.2, 1.2.3+build.5 or 1.2.3-rc.1+b7. MAJOR, MINOR and PATCH are non-negative decimal integers without leading zeros ("0" is fine, "01" is not) and can be longer than 15 digits. The prerelease is one or more identifiers joined by dots; an identifier is a non-empty run of the characters 0-9, A-Z, a-z and hyphen, and an identifier made only of digits has no leading zeros. The build metadata is one or more non-empty identifiers of the same characters (leading zeros are fine) and is ignored everywhere. No spaces are allowed inside a version. Precedence of two versions: compare MAJOR, MINOR and PATCH as integers; if they are equal, a version with a prerelease is lower than the same version without one; if both have a prerelease, compare the identifiers from left to right: two numeric identifiers compare as integers, two other identifiers compare by character code order, a numeric identifier is lower than any other identifier, and if all shared identifiers are equal the version with fewer identifiers is lower. A range is one or more sets joined by ||; spaces or tabs around || and at both ends of the range are ignored; an empty set is malformed. A set is one or more comparators separated by spaces or tabs, and a version satisfies the set when it satisfies every comparator and the prerelease rule below. A comparator is an optional operator directly followed by a version, with no space between them: >=V, <=V, >V, <V, =V, plain V (it means the same as =V; equal means equal precedence), ~V and ^V. ~V means >=V and <MAJOR.(MINOR+1).0. ^V means >=V and below the first of: (MAJOR+1).0.0 when MAJOR is above 0; 0.(MINOR+1).0 when MAJOR is 0 and MINOR is above 0; 0.0.(PATCH+1) when MAJOR and MINOR are both 0. The upper limits written like 2.0.0 have no prerelease. Prerelease rule: a version that has a prerelease satisfies a set only if at least one comparator of that set has a version with a prerelease and the same MAJOR, MINOR and PATCH as the tested version. For ~ and ^ that comparator version is V itself, not the upper limit. A version without a prerelease is not affected by this rule. A range is satisfied when at least one of its sets is satisfied.

edges.prerelease-numeric: two numeric identifiers compare as integers
edges.prerelease-kinds: a numeric identifier is lower than any other identifier
edges.prerelease-length: the version with fewer identifiers is lower

input.name: sumRepeatingDecimals
input.task: Add decimal numbers that may have a repeating part and return the exact sum. terms is an array of strings. Every term is well formed and has one of these shapes, with an optional leading minus sign: I (an integer), I.F (a finite decimal), I.(R) (a decimal whose digits after the point are all repeating) or I.F(R) (a finite part followed by a repeating block). I, F and R are non-empty strings of decimal digits; they can have leading zeros, and each can be up to 60 digits long. The part in parentheses repeats forever, so "0.(3)" is 1/3, "1.2(45)" is 1.2454545... = 137/110 and "0.(9)" is exactly 1. Return the exact sum as a reduced fraction: "p/q" with q greater than 1 and no common factor of p and q, or just "p" when the sum is an integer. A negative sum has the minus sign in front of p ("-1/3"). A zero sum, also for an empty terms array, is "0".

edges.reduced: no common factor of p and q
edges.negative: minus sign in front of p

input.name: unionIntervals
input.task: Each element of list is a string for an interval of real numbers: "[a,b]", "[a,b)", "(a,b]" or "(a,b)", where a and b are integers written in decimal without spaces, a plus sign or leading zeros (they can be negative; their absolute value is at most 10^15). A square bracket includes its end point and a round bracket excludes it. The interval holds real numbers, not only integers: "(1,2)" is not empty. An interval is empty and is ignored when a > b, or when a = b and the interval is not "[a,a]" (so "[3,3]" is the single point 3, while "(3,3)", "[3,3)" and "[5,2]" are empty). Return the union of all the intervals as the shortest possible array of strings in the same format, sorted from left to right, where no two result intervals overlap or can be merged. Two intervals merge when they overlap, or when they meet at one end point value and at least one of the two brackets at that value is square ("[1,2)" and "[2,3]" give "[1,3]"; "[1,2]" and "(2,3]" give "[1,3]"; "[1,2)" and "(2,3]" stay apart because the point 2 is missing; "[1,2)" and "[2,2]" give "[1,2]"). An empty list, or a list with only empty intervals, gives an empty array.

edges.touching: at least one of the two brackets at that value is square

input.name: areaCoveredAtLeast
input.task: Each element of rects is [x1, y1, x2, y2], the corners of an axis-aligned rectangle with integer coordinates whose absolute value is at most 10^9; the two corners can come in any order (x1 can be larger than x2, and y1 can be larger than y2). rects has at most 40 elements. A rectangle with zero width or zero height has no area and counts for nothing. Return the total area of the region that is covered by at least k of the rectangles (area is counted once, however many rectangles cover it), as a decimal string. k is an integer from 1 to 40; if k is larger than the number of rectangles the area is 0. The area can be larger than 2^53, so return it exactly. Rectangles that only share a border cover no common area.

edges.k-too-large: if k is larger than the number of rectangles

input.name: classifyPoints
input.task: polygon is an array of [x, y] integer vertices (3 to 60 vertices, coordinates with absolute value at most 10^9) listed in order, clockwise or counter-clockwise, describing a simple polygon: its edges join each vertex to the next and the last to the first, they never cross or touch except at shared consecutive end points, and no vertex repeats. Three or more consecutive vertices can lie on one straight line. The polygon can be concave. points is an array of [x, y] integer points with the same limits. Return an array with one string for each point: "boundary" when the point lies on an edge (including every vertex), otherwise "inside" when it lies in the interior of the polygon, otherwise "outside". Be exact: products of such coordinates exceed 2^53.

input.name: roundRobin
input.task: Simulate one CPU that shares its time between jobs in round-robin order. jobs is an array of [id, arrival, burst]: id is a unique string, arrival is the integer time when the job becomes ready (0 or more) and burst is the integer amount of CPU time it needs (1 or more). jobs is not sorted. quantum is an integer of 1 or more. Rules. The ready queue is first in, first out. When the CPU is free it takes the job at the front of the queue and runs it for min(quantum, remaining time) time units. If the job has time left afterwards, it goes to the back of the queue; otherwise it finishes at the current time. Switching jobs costs no time. If the queue is empty the CPU idles until the next job arrives. A job enters the queue at its arrival time. When several things happen at the same time t, the order is: first every job that arrives at a time less than or equal to t and is not yet queued enters the queue (earlier arrival times first; jobs with the same arrival time enter in the order in which they appear in jobs), and only then the job that just used up its quantum at time t goes to the back of the queue. This also holds for a job that arrives exactly when the CPU becomes free. Return an array of [id, finishTime] in the order in which the jobs finish. An empty jobs array gives an empty array.

edges.arrival-before-requeue: and only then the job that just used up its quantum
edges.same-arrival-order: enter in the order in which they appear in jobs
edges.exact-finish: otherwise it finishes at the current time
edges.free-cpu-arrival: a job that arrives exactly when the CPU becomes free

input.name: matchOrders
input.task: Simulate a limit order book. orders is an array that is processed in order; each element is one of: ["L", id, side, price, qty] (limit order), ["M", id, side, qty] (market order) or ["X", id] (cancel). id is a string, side is "B" (buy) or "S" (sell), price and qty are positive integers, and each id is used by at most one L or M order. Matching. An incoming buy order trades against resting sell orders, and an incoming sell order against resting buy orders. A limit buy only trades with resting sells whose price is at most its price; a limit sell only with resting buys whose price is at least its price; a market order accepts any price. The best resting order is matched first: the lowest price for an incoming buy, the highest price for an incoming sell; among equal prices the one that arrived earlier goes first. Each match is a trade of min(remaining incoming quantity, remaining resting quantity) units at the price of the resting order, never the incoming order's limit price. Keep matching until the incoming order is filled or no acceptable resting order is left. A limit order with quantity left then rests in the book and keeps its place by price and arrival; a market order with quantity left is dropped and never rests. Cancel removes the resting order with that id (with whatever quantity is left); if there is no such resting order (unknown id, an order that is already filled, or a market order) nothing happens. Return an object {trades, bids, asks}. trades lists every trade in order as [takerId, makerId, price, qty]. bids and asks describe the book after all orders: one [price, totalRemainingQty] per price level, bids from the highest price to the lowest, asks from the lowest price to the highest; empty levels are not listed.

edges.maker-price: never the incoming order's limit price
edges.time-priority: the one that arrived earlier goes first
edges.price-priority: the lowest price for an incoming buy
edges.market-any-price: a market order accepts any price

input.name: simulateCache
input.task: Simulate a cache that holds at most capacity entries and forgets entries after ttl time units. capacity and ttl are integers of 1 or more. ops is an array of operations in order; each is ["put", time, key, value], ["get", time, key] or ["size", time]. time is an integer and never decreases from one operation to the next. key is a string; value is any JSON value other than null. An entry written at time w is expired at time t when t - w >= ttl. Before each operation, every entry that is expired at that operation's time is removed. put: if key is in the cache, overwrite its value and set its write time to the current time, and make it the most recently used entry; otherwise add it as the most recently used entry, and if the cache now holds more than capacity entries, remove the least recently used one. get: if key is in the cache, return its value and make it the most recently used entry, but do not change its write time (reading does not extend its life); otherwise return null. size: return the number of entries in the cache. The result is an array with one element per operation, in order: null for put, the value or null for get, and a number for size.

edges.purge: every entry that is expired at that operation
edges.overwrite: overwrite its value and set its write time
edges.lru-eviction: remove the least recently used one
edges.get-recency: make it the most recently used entry
edges.get-no-refresh: reading does not extend its life
edges.size: return the number of entries in the cache

input.name: cheapestWithCoupons
input.signature: cheapestWithCoupons(n, edges, k, from, to) -> number
input.task: Find the cheapest way to travel in a directed graph when you have coupons. The graph has n nodes numbered 0 to n-1 (1 <= n <= 300). edges is an array of [u, v, w]: a directed edge from u to v that costs w, an integer from 0 to 1000000000 (w can be 0). There can be several edges between the same two nodes, and edges from a node to itself. You may use up to k coupons (k is an integer from 0 to 30). A coupon is used on one crossing of one edge and changes the cost of that crossing from w to floor(w / 2); one crossing can use at most one coupon, and an edge that is crossed twice needs a coupon each time. Using fewer than k coupons is allowed. Return the minimum total cost to go from node from to node to, or -1 if to cannot be reached from from. If from equals to the cost is 0. Note that the cheapest way without coupons is not always the cheapest way with them.

edges.parallel: several edges between the same two nodes
edges.same-node: If from equals to the cost is 0
edges.fewer-coupons: Using fewer than k coupons is allowed
edges.route-changes: not always the cheapest way with them

input.name: earlyLabelOrder
input.task: nodes is an array of distinct strings (1 to 200 entries). edges is an array of [a, b] pairs with both a and b taken from nodes; each pair means that a must appear before b in the order. The same pair can appear more than once. Return an order of all the nodes that follows every edge and is the best by this rule. Sort the labels in ascending order, s1 < s2 < s3 < ..., comparing strings by UTF-16 code unit as the JavaScript < operator does (so "10" < "9" and "B" < "a"). Among all valid orders choose the one in which s1 stands at the earliest possible position; among those, the one in which s2 stands at the earliest possible position; and so on. This is not the same as the order that is smallest when read from left to right. Return null if no valid order exists, which happens exactly when the edges contain a cycle (including an edge [a, a]).

edges.left-to-right: smallest when read from left to right
edges.null-on-cycle: Return null if no valid order exists
